content:
One version of events about how a former Apple employee obtained company secrets before leaving for OpenAI has been undermined by a court filing.

It was speculated that the employee may have obtained documents without knowledge due to chaotic iCloud arrangements for Apple staff — but Apple says that's not what happened…

Quick recap

Apple sued OpenAI last month, accusing the company of theft of trade secrets related to a hardware project. One key accusation involves a former Apple employee named Chang Liu, who had since moved to OpenAI. Here is a brief timeline of events:

  • July 10: Apple files lawsuit against OpenAI, accusing former Apple staff of systematically stealing Apple trade secrets to benefit OpenAI's future hardware efforts
  • July 10: OpenAI issues brief response denying allegations
  • July 14: OpenAI updates response, saying it has seen no evidence to support Apple's claims
  • August 3: OpenAI publishes blog post attacking Apple's lawsuit
  • August 4: Apple files for temporary restraining order to avoid "irreparable harm"

The iCloud mess

OpenAI claims that it was an Apple security lapse that allowed former employees to retain access to what were supposedly "unwanted" secret files after they left.

Earlier this week, The Information published a report suggesting this may have been due to chaotic iCloud arrangements.

The report says that while Apple removes former employees' access to company-managed iCloud folders, many files likely had been shared to Apple employees' personal accounts — and these employees not only still had access to these files after they left, but may have continued to receive update push notifications.

In other words, former employees may have been receiving push notifications of secret file updates on their personal devices, without any wrongdoing on their part.

Apple says it's not related

However, John Gruber at Daring Fireball notes that Apple made it clear in their court filing that the files in question were not stored on iCloud.

Gruber suggests the files were most likely stored on Box — a cloud storage service used widely by Apple.

9to5Mac's take

For now, it's just a case of he said, she said, she said. We'll have to wait for a trial to sort out the fact from the fiction.

However, this iCloud arrangement issue does appear to be tacitly acknowledged by Apple. The arrangement, we understand, exists to prevent Apple employees from needing to carry both a personal and a work iPhone. While understandable, it is certainly a significant security hole.
